```{r main-analysis}
# ---- Main study: identical to the registered PAP Version 2 code ----
set.seed(111626)

topics <- c("morning routine", "night routine", "meal prep", "cleaning routine",
            "grocery haul", "sourdough bread", "baking from scratch",
            "skincare routine", "makeup tutorial", "hair care routine",
            "outfit ideas", "home decor", "garden tour", "homeschooling",
            "parenting tips", "toddler activities", "pregnancy tips",
            "marriage advice", "dating advice", "wedding planning",
            "budgeting tips", "laundry routine", "home organization",
            "easy dinner recipes", "sewing for beginners",
            "knitting for beginners", "workout routine", "self care routine",
            "day in the life", "kitchen tour")

n_units <- 30
n_treat <- 15
n_top   <- 20
n_sims  <- 10000
frame   <- "tradwife"

Z <- complete_ra(N = n_units, m = n_treat)
assignments <- data.frame(
  topic_id = 1:n_units,
  topic    = topics,
  Z        = Z,
  query    = ifelse(Z == 1, paste(frame, topics), topics),
  order    = sample(1:n_units)
) |>
  arrange(order)

results <- read.csv("search_results.csv")

dat <- results |>
  filter(rank <= n_top) |>
  group_by(topic_id) |>
  summarise(Y = sum(political), n_results = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(assignments, by = "topic_id") |>
  mutate(condition = factor(Z, levels = 0:1,
                            labels = c("Neutral query", "Conservative-coded query")))

fit <- difference_in_means(Y ~ Z, data = dat)

declaration <- declare_ra(N = n_units, m = n_treat)
ri_h1 <- conduct_ri(Y ~ Z, declaration = declaration, assignment = "Z",
                    sharp_hypothesis = 0, sims = n_sims, p = "upper",
                    data = dat)

results_table <- data.frame(
  estimate  = fit$coefficients, std.error = fit$std.error,
  conf.low  = fit$conf.low,     conf.high = fit$conf.high,
  ri_p_one_tailed = summary(ri_h1)$upper_p_value
)
```

```{r inline-values}
fmt   <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p == 0, paste0("< ", format(1 / n_sims, scientific = FALSE)),
                            formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 4))

# ---- Core estimates -------------------------------------------------
ate    <- fmt(results_table$estimate)           # ATE (1.47)
se     <- fmt(results_table$std.error)          # Neyman SE (0.39)
ci_lo  <- fmt(results_table$conf.low)           # 95% CI lower (0.64)
ci_hi  <- fmt(results_table$conf.high)          # 95% CI upper (2.29)
p_ri   <- fmt_p(results_table$ri_p_one_tailed)  # one-tailed RI p (0.0002)
p_t <- fmt_p(fit$p.value)   # two-tailed Welch t-test p (0.0016)

# ---- Randomization inference details ----------------------------------
ri_sims      <- ri_h1$sims_df$est_sim
n_sims_fmt   <- format(n_sims, big.mark = ",")                               # "10,000"
n_ri_extreme <- sum(ri_sims >= results_table$estimate - 1e-8)                # sims >= observed (2)
ri_max_sim   <- fmt(max(ri_sims))                                            # largest simulated ATE

# ---- Outcomes by condition --------------------------------------------
y_c <- dat$Y[dat$Z == 0]; y_t <- dat$Y[dat$Z == 1]
n_c      <- length(y_c);           n_t      <- length(y_t)         # topics per arm
mean_c   <- fmt(mean(y_c));        mean_t   <- fmt(mean(y_t))      # means 
sd_c     <- fmt(sd(y_c));          sd_t     <- fmt(sd(y_t))        # SDs 
max_c    <- max(y_c);              max_t    <- max(y_t)            # max per topic
sum_c    <- sum(y_c);              sum_t    <- sum(y_t)            # political results/arm
any_c    <- sum(y_c > 0);          any_t    <- sum(y_t > 0)        # topics with >= 1
pct_c    <- fmt(100 * sum_c / (n_c * n_top), 1)                    # % of control results
pct_t    <- fmt(100 * sum_t / (n_t * n_top), 1)                    # % of treated results
ratio_tc <- fmt(mean(y_t) / mean(y_c), 1)                          # treated mean / control 

# ---- Data collection ---------------------------------------------------
coding_log   <- read.csv("search_coding_log.csv")
n_results    <- nrow(results)                                      # results coded
n_pol        <- sum(results$political)                             # coded political
pct_pol      <- fmt(100 * n_pol / n_results, 1)                    # % political overall 
n_unique_vid <- length(unique(results$video_id))                   # distinct videos
n_unique_pol <- length(unique(results$video_id[results$political == 1])) # pol vid 
n_borderline <- sum(coding_log$borderline == 1)                    # flagged borderline
times_et     <- as.POSIXct(results$searched_at, format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%OSZ", tz = "UTC")
search_date  <- format(min(times_et), "%B %d, %Y", tz = "America/New_York")   # November 15, 2026
search_start <- format(min(times_et), "%I:%M %p", tz = "America/New_York")    # 11:11 PM (ET)
search_end   <- format(max(times_et), "%I:%M %p", tz = "America/New_York")    # 11:14 PM (ET)
search_mins  <- fmt(as.numeric(difftime(max(times_et), min(times_et), units = "mins")), 1)

# ---- Exploratory sensitivity check -------------------------------------
judgment_ids <- unique(results$video_id[grepl("borderline, coded 1", results$note)])
fit_strict   <- results |>
  mutate(political = ifelse(video_id %in% judgment_ids, 0, political)) |>
  group_by(topic_id) |> summarise(Y = sum(political), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(assignments, by = "topic_id") |>
  difference_in_means(Y ~ Z, data = _)
n_judgment   <- length(judgment_ids)                    # videos recoded
ate_strict   <- fmt(fit_strict$coefficients)           
se_strict    <- fmt(fit_strict$std.error)             
ci_lo_strict <- fmt(fit_strict$conf.low)            
ci_hi_strict <- fmt(fit_strict$conf.high)        

# ---- Pilot (TikTok) -----------------------------------------------------
# Names follow a{account}r{round}_{stat}, e.g. a1r1_likes = account 1, round 1
pilot_assign <- read_excel("practicum_data.xlsx", sheet = "assignments") |> select(account, Z1, Z2)
pilot_vid    <- read_excel("practicum_data.xlsx", sheet = "videos") |>
  filter(account %in% c(1, 2), !is.na(likes)) |>
  group_by(account, round) |>
  summarise(n = n(), likes = mean(likes), comments = mean(comments),
            followers = mean(followers), .groups = "drop")

comma <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",")
for (i in seq_len(nrow(pilot_vid))) {
  k <- paste0("a", pilot_vid$account[i], "r", pilot_vid$round[i])
  assign(paste0(k, "_n"),             pilot_vid$n[i])                          # videos
  assign(paste0(k, "_likes"),         comma(pilot_vid$likes[i]))               # mean likes
  assign(paste0(k, "_comments"),      comma(pilot_vid$comments[i]))            # mean comments
  assign(paste0(k, "_followers"),     comma(pilot_vid$followers[i]))           # mean followers
  assign(paste0(k, "_log_likes"),     fmt(log(pilot_vid$likes[i] + 1), 1))     # log(mean + 1)
  assign(paste0(k, "_log_comments"),  fmt(log(pilot_vid$comments[i] + 1), 1))
  assign(paste0(k, "_log_followers"), fmt(log(pilot_vid$followers[i] + 1), 1))
}
# Creates: a1r1_*, a1r2_*, a2r1_*, a2r2_*
# Account 1: round 1 conservative, round 2 cockapoo. Account 2: both rounds conservative.

# Pooled by content type (all liked videos from accounts 1-2)
pilot_pool <- read_excel("practicum_data.xlsx", sheet = "videos") |>
  filter(account %in% c(1, 2), !is.na(likes)) |>
  left_join(pilot_assign, by = "account") |>
  mutate(cons = if_else(round == 1, Z1, Z2) == 1)
cons_likes         <- comma(mean(pilot_pool$likes[pilot_pool$cons]))       # conservative-coded
cockapoo_likes     <- comma(mean(pilot_pool$likes[!pilot_pool$cons]))      # cockapoo
cons_followers     <- comma(mean(pilot_pool$followers[pilot_pool$cons]))
cockapoo_followers <- comma(mean(pilot_pool$followers[!pilot_pool$cons]))
n_pilot_videos     <- nrow(pilot_pool)                                     # 299
```

# Introduction

Recent anecdotal evidence [@liscomb2025] has alluded to the existence of
an alt-right "pipeline" on social media platforms, whereby apolitical
social and/or lifestyle content may contain references to
ideologically-extreme viewpoints. Though previous research has studied
how recommendation systems on YouTube [@brown] and Twitter (now X;
@huszár2022) amplify political content, this study examines one entry
point to that pipeline: search. Specifically, the project examines
whether content that aligns with conservative ideological themes, but is
not itself political, leads platforms to present users with content that
directly implicates conservative or political beliefs.

This practicum experiment consists of two methodological components: an
earlier-planned field experiment employing 30 individual accounts on
TikTok, and a randomized search experiment on YouTube. This dual-pronged
approach became necessary as only two accounts completed the initial
design before TikTok blocked logins to every study account and blocked
the creation of new ones on November 15, 2026. As such, the main content
of the practicum explores whether, when a user frames an ordinary
lifestyle search in conservative-coded terms, the platform returns more
explicitly political content. Therefore, the research hypothesis I am
testing is as follows:

> **Hypothesis 1:** YouTube searches for lifestyle topics that include a
> conservative-coded frame ("tradwife") will return more explicitly
> political videos among the top 20 results than searches for the same
> kind of topic without the frame.

# Research Design

For this experiment, I collected data on 30 lifestyle search topics,
chosen before randomization to be ordinary, apolitical searches about
domestic life, appearance, family and relationships. Each topic
represented one unit and was searched exactly once, in either its
treated or its control form. Table 1 lists each topic, its condition,
and the query used.

```{r tab-design}
assignments |>
  arrange(desc(Z), topic) |>
  transmute(Topic = topic,
            Condition = ifelse(Z == 1, "Treatment", "Control"),
            `Query searched` = query,
            `Search order` = order) |>
  kable(caption = "Search topics, random assignment, and search order",
        row.names = FALSE)
```

Here, the treatment represents a conservative-coded frame added to the
start of the search query. A treated topic was searched as "tradwife
*topic*" (for example, "tradwife morning routine"). A control topic was
searched as the topic alone ("morning routine"). "Tradwife" was used
because it was the hashtag most associated with conservative gender-role
content in the pilot \@[@liscomb2025], and it is not itself a political
term. The two forms of the query were otherwise identical. No covariates
were collected, as the topic list was fixed before assignment, so
randomization alone balanced the arms in expectation.

The outcome measured was the number of **explicitly political videos
among the first 20 video results** on the first results page with the
"Videos" filter applied, so it represented a count from 0 to 20. Ads,
channel results, playlists and grouped shelves were excluded. A given
result was considered to be "explicitly political" if its title, channel
name or description snippet, as shown on the results page, contained any
of the following attributes:[^1]

[^1]: Content about gender roles, religion or wellness with no explicit
    political reference was coded 0. The same rule was used for pilot
    accounts 2 and 3.

- naming a politician, political party, election, law or government
  policy, or political movement (such as MAHA or feminism as a
  movement); or
- openly arguing a political position.

All 30 searches were run in a single sitting on November 15, 2026. Each
search loaded YouTube's public results page (`youtube.com/results`),
with language set to English, region set to the US, and YouTube's
"Videos" type filter applied) in a fresh, signed-out request that
carried no cookies, search history or watch history. Each query
therefore reached YouTube as a new, anonymous visitor. Furthermore, all
requests came from the same network and device, with the date and time
of every search also recorded in the data. If a request failed or
returned fewer than 20 videos, it was repeated after a short pause, up
to three times, and the number of attempts was recorded. If 20 results
were not returned, the outcome was counted over the results that were
returned, and the shortfall was reported.

Assignment used complete random assignment (`complete_ra`) with the
`randomizr` package on R [@blair2019]. 15 topics were assigned to
treatment and 15 to control, with no blocking or clustering. The order
in which the 30 searches are run was also randomized, separately, so
that time of search was not confounded with treatment.

## Core Assumptions

**Random assignment** is satisfied by the design procedure, which
employs complete random assignment with a fixed seed to ensure
replicability.

**Excludability** is satisfied, as the only difference between the two
conditions is the word "tradwife" in the query, as seen above in
Table 1. All searches use the same settings, the same time window and
the same procedure.

**Non-interference** is satisfied given that each request is
cookie-free, so one search is not expected to change another unit's
results through search history. All requests shared one IP address and
ran within a short period, so some interference through network-level
personalization cannot be ruled out. Running the searches in random
order should keep any such drift from lining up with treatment.

**Non-compliance** is not expected, as this would entail the failure of
the YouTube search algorithm to produce any recommended videos in
response to a given query. As each of the selected topics represents a
broad topic for which I expect multiple videos to exist, there is no
supporting evidence to suggest that this would occur.

**Attrition** is not expected because there is no evidence of
algorithmic refusal to provide any recommendations for social topics on
YouTube [@brown]. Whereas most social media platforms have implemented
content restrictions to limit algorithmic behavior from recommending
topics that may promote norm-violating behaviors or attitudes [@meta],
there is no supporting evidence to suggest that topics solely
referencing aspects of daily life would be flagged for such violations.

# Results

Figure 1 reports the frequency distribution for the number of explicitly
political videos among the top 20 videos recommended by YouTube's
algorithm. Among neutral queries, i.e., those containing the topic
alone, the modal value of explicitly political videos out of 20
recommended was equal to zero (`r sum(y_c == 0)` search terms), with the
remaining `r sum(y_c == 1)` search terms returning exactly one
explicitly political video out of the 20 recommended. The total number
of explicitly political videos recommended in response to neutral
queries was `r sum_c`.

Meanwhile, among conservative-coded queries, i.e., those containing the
topic plus the phrase `tradwife`, `r sum(y_t == 0)` search terms
returned zero explicitly political videos. This indicates that
`r sum(y_c == 1)` neutral topics and `r sum(y_t >= 1)`
conservative-coded topics returned at least one explicitly political
video out of the 20 recommended. The total number of explicitly
political videos recommended was `r sum_t`. Together, the range of
values for the number of explicitly political videos within the control
group was `r max_c`, whereas the range of values for the number of
explicitly political videos within the treatment group was `r max_t`.

```{r fig-dist, fig.cap="Frequency of Explicitly Political Videos Among Top 20 Recommended"}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = Y)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~ condition, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:n_top, limits = c(-0.5, n_top + 0.5)) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Number of videos",
       y = "Number of topics")
```

Table 2 displays the mean number of explicitly political videos among
the top 20 recommended results on YouTube in the control and treatment
conditions. Among neutral queries, there were `r mean_c` recommended
videos on average that contained explicitly political content (*SD* =
`r sd_c`), comprising around `r pct_c`% of the total videos within this
condition.

Conversely, among conservative-coded queries, there were `r mean_t`
recommended videos on average that contained explicitly political
content (*SD* = `r sd_t`), comprising around `r pct_t`% of the total
videos within this condition. This indicates that conservative-coded
queries are more likely to result in the presence of explicitly
political content within the first 20 recommended videos on YouTube, as
opposed to neutral queries.

```{r tab-means}
dat |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  summarise(Topics = n(), Mean = mean(Y), SD = sd(Y),
            Min = min(Y), Max = max(Y), .groups = "drop") |>
  rename(Condition = condition) |>
  kable(digits = 2,
        caption = "Explicitly Political Videos Among Top 20 Recommended, By Condition")
```

Table 3 summarizes the main results of this experiment, in which I
estimate the average treatment effect (ATE) of adding the
conservative-coded frame on the number of explicitly political videos
among the top 20 results, across the 30 topics. Using a difference in
means estimator, I find the ATE is `r ate` (*SE* = `r se`), which
represents a substantial increase in the prevalence of explicitly
political videos recommended to users. Specifically, on average, the
treatment group's recommendations contained `r ratio_tc` times more
explicitly political videos than the control group's recommendations.

I test the statistical significance of this result using a a one-tailed
randomization inference test under the sharp null hypothesis, which
states that the effect of conservative-coded queries on the number of
recommended videos containing explicitly political content is zero for
all issues included in the sample. As the hypothesis specifies a
direction of the estimated effect, a one-tailed test is used.

Across 10,000 simulated assignments, the reported p-value for this
estimate is `r p_ri`, which indicates that the probability of obtaining
an ATE at least as large as the estimate observed is
`r fmt(results_table$ri_p_one_tailed * 100)` percent. Notably, the
conventional two-tailed t-test gives the same conclusion (*p* =
`r p_t`). Therefore, I can reject the sharp null hypothesis that there
is no effect for any query.

```{r tab-results}
data.frame(
  `ATE`               = results_table$estimate,
  `SE`                = results_table$std.error,
  `95% CI`            = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", results_table$conf.low,
                                results_table$conf.high),
  `p (one-tailed)` = fmt_p(results_table$ri_p_one_tailed),
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  kable(digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
        caption = paste0("Estimated Average Treatment Effect of Conservative-Coded Framing"))
```

Figure 2 showcases the randomization inference in graphical form. Here,
I identify the simulated ATE as `r ate`, with a 95% confidence interval
of [`r ci_lo`, `r ci_hi`]. This indicates that 95% of all confidence
intervals simulated under the same schedule of potential outcomes will
produce an interval containing the true ATE. Since the generated
confidence interval does not overlap with zero, I can conclude that my
hypothesis is supported, meaning conservative-coded queries have a
greater effect on exposure to explicitly political content within the
first 20 recommended videos on YouTube than neutral queries.

```{r fig-ri, fig.cap="Randomization Inference"}
plot(ri_h1) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = "Simulated ATE under the sharp null")
```

*Note.* Distribution of simulated ATEs under the sharp null of no effect
(10,000 simulations). The vertical line marks the observed ATE.

Lastly, Figure 3 presents a visualization of the experimental results,
in the style of (my former advisor) @coppock2021. In comparing the two
experimental groups, there is a marked increase between neural and
conservative-coded queries on the mean number of explicitly political
videos out of the top 20 recommended results on YouTube, which is
consistent with the earlier-reported findings. Furthermore, the 95%
confidence intervals do not overlap, suggesting a limited range of
uncertainty in the estimates.

```{r fig-coppock, fig.cap="Visualization of Explicitly Political Videos Among Top 20 Recommended, By Condition"}
fit_means <- lm_robust(Y ~ 0 + condition, data = dat)
means_df <- data.frame(
  condition = factor(levels(dat$condition), levels = levels(dat$condition)),
  Y = unname(fit_means$coefficients),
  conf.low = unname(fit_means$conf.low), conf.high = unname(fit_means$conf.high)
)
ggplot(means_df, aes(condition, Y)) +
  geom_point(data = dat, position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0.1),
             alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.5, n_top), breaks = seq(0, n_top, 2)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_blank()) +
  ylab("Explicitly political videos\n(of top 20 YouTube results)")
```

*Note.* Points are individual topics; black dots are condition means
with 95% confidence intervals.

# Conclusion

Though recent anecdotal evidence points to an alt-right "pipeline" on
social media, in which apolitical lifestyle content can carry references
to ideologically extreme viewpoints, it is unclear how this process
plays out among everyday users. Therefore, in this experiment, I sought
to observe this phenomeon by directly testing how searching for
conservative-coded social content may affect the prevalence of
explicitly political content recommended by YouTube.

The results support the hypothesis that there is a meaningful
algorithmic pathway between content that aligns with conservative
ideological themes and that which directly implicates conservative or
political beliefs. This means that YouTube searches for lifestyle topics
that include a conservative-coded frame will return more explicitly
political videos among the top 20 results than searches for the same
kind of topic without that frame.

Overall, this project contributes to the nascence of literature that has
only begun observing the relationship between exposure to social content
that aligns with conservative ideological themes and the propensity by
which algorithmic feed designs on YouTube, [@brown], Twitter (now X;
@huszár2022), and TikTok [@shin2024] present users with social and
political content that directly implicates conservative ideological
beliefs. Furthermore, determining whether variations in the amount of
social media content viewed containing conservative-coded social topics
alter the algorithm's presentation frequency of explicitly, politically
conservative content, for instance, may provide fruitful insights into
the process by which the algorithm is able to generate more accurate
predictions of user engagement.

Table 5 indicates the specific search query that produced a given video

The coding was done with the help of the Opus 5.5 AI model, developed by

# Appendix B: Initial Study (TikTok)

The initial practicum sought to establish 30 new TikTok accounts with no
followers or following. Each account would like 25 videos for each of
three hashtags in each of two rounds. Treatment accounts liked videos
from conservative-coded hashtags (#cleanbeauty, #tradwife, #softliving);
control accounts liked videos from apolitical cockapoo hashtags
(#cockapoo, #cockapoosoftiktok, #cockapoolife). Each round was assigned
by its own independent complete random assignment (15/15). The outcome
was the number of explicitly political videos among the first 50 "For
You" videos, measured at baseline, after round 1 and after round 2.
Version 1 posed two hypotheses:

> **H1:** accounts that interact with conservative-coded content will
> have more explicitly political content on their "For You" page than
> accounts that interact with apolitical content.
>
> **H2:** accounts that interact with more conservative-coded content
> overall will have more explicitly political content on their "For You"
> page than accounts that interact with less.

However, on 2026-11-15, during data collection, TikTok blocked logins to
every study account and blocked new accounts from being created, so no
further data could be collected. TikTok gave no reason. A likely factor
is that all accounts were run from one device and network, which
platforms commonly treat as coordinated multi-account activity, but this
cannot be confirmed. Data collection stopped as follows:

| Account | $Z_1$ | $Z_2$ | Waves measured | Liked-video rows | Status             |
|:-------:|:-----:|:-----:|:--------------:|:----------------:|:-------------------|
|    1    |   1   |   0   |    0, 1, 2     |    150 / 150     | Complete$^\dagger$ |
|    2    |   1   |   1   |    0, 1, 2     |    149 / 150     | Complete$^\dagger$ |
|    3    |   1   |   0   |       0        |     0 / 150      | Baseline only      |

\vspace{-12pt}

Note. Pilot data completeness. Accounts 4–30 have no data.
$^\dagger$With the deviations listed below.

\bigskip

The following departures from the Version 1 protocol occurred:

1.  **Outcome videos were saved (accounts 1 and 2).** Every "For You"
    video counted at each wave was also bookmarked to Favorites. That is
    an engagement signal that may have shaped the next wave's feed.
2.  **Treatment videos were saved as well as liked (accounts 1 and 2).**
3.  **Most of account 2's likes did not register.** TikTok's page data
    shows 58 of 150 treatment videos liked (none in round 2), although
    all 150 were saved.
4.  **Account 3's likes did not persist.** The account searched
    #cleanbeauty and viewed 25 videos. Its likes were confirmed at the
    time but did not appear in TikTok's data afterwards, and wave 1 was
    never measured.
5.  **Account 2's video counts were read after the fact**, on
    2026-11-15. Values of 10,000 or more are rounded by TikTok.
6.  **Account 1's coding was done by the researcher** before the coding
    rule in Part II was written down. Accounts 2 and 3 were coded with
    that rule.
7.  **All accounts shared one device and network**, which weakens the
    assumption that the accounts are independent.

With one complete account per round-2 condition, and every account with
data assigned to treatment in round 1, H1 and H2 could not be tested.
Even the smallest possible randomization inference $p$-value was 0.5.
The pilot results are therefore reported descriptively only.

```{r pilot-analysis}
p_assign <- read_excel("practicum_data.xlsx", sheet = "assignments") |>
  select(account, Z1, Z2) |> mutate(rounds = Z1 + Z2)
p_out    <- read_excel("practicum_data.xlsx", sheet = "outcomes")
p_videos <- read_excel("practicum_data.xlsx", sheet = "videos")

pilot <- p_assign |> left_join(p_out, by = "account")
pilot_complete <- pilot |>
  filter(!is.na(pol_wave0), !is.na(pol_wave1), !is.na(pol_wave2))
```

The below figure denotes the mean number of explicitly political videos
observed across each wave:

```{r pilot-traj-plot, fig.cap="Number of Explicitly Political 'For You' Videos Across Waves", fig.height=4.5}
pilot_complete |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("pol_wave"), names_to = "wave",
               names_prefix = "pol_wave", values_to = "political") |>
  mutate(account = factor(paste("Account", account, "| Rounds Treated =", rounds))) |>
  ggplot(aes(wave, political, group = account, linetype = account)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 50)) + theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.direction = "vertical") +
  labs(x = "Wave",
       y = "Explicitly political videos",
       linetype = NULL)
```

*Note.* Wave 0 = baseline; Wave 1 = after round 1; Wave 2 = after round
2. Explicitly political videos measured as function of $n/50$ 'For You'
videos. Data for Accounts 1 and 2 only.

Elsewhere, I collected a set of descriptive statistics for the following
values:

- `likes`: This represents the total number of likes (excluding that of
  the user account) on that video.

- `comments`: This represents the total number of comments (of which the
  user account will leave none) on that video.

- `followers`: This represents the total number of other accounts
  (excluding that of the user account) that are following the account
  which posted the video.

To ensure that there are no potential confounding effects of increased
time spent on an account's profile page, I collected these measurements
on a separate device. I created a composite score for likes, comments,
and followers, respectively, by calculating the mean value across all
150 videos. I then applied logarithmic transformation to these
variables. The below table indicates the calculated statistics by
account and condition:

```{r pilot-videos-table}
cell <- function(m) sprintf("%s (%.1f)", format(round(m), big.mark = ","), log(m + 1))

p_videos |>
  filter(account %in% pilot_complete$account, !is.na(likes)) |>
  left_join(p_assign, by = "account") |>
  mutate(condition = if_else(if_else(round == 1, Z1, Z2) == 1,
                             "Conservative", "Cockapoo")) |>
  group_by(account, round, condition) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            Likes     = cell(mean(likes)),
            Comments  = cell(mean(comments)),
            Followers = cell(mean(followers)),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  rename(Account = account, Round = round, Content = condition, Videos = n) |>
  kable(align = "cccrrrr",
        caption = "Mean Likes, Comments, and Creator Followers for Liked Videos By Account and Round")
```

*Note.* Logarithmic value of mean provided in parentheses. One Account 2
video (round 1, #cleanbeauty) was unavailable.

The total sample size of videos watched was `` `r n_pilot_videos` ``.
Within this sample, videos liked in the cockapoo-coded condition
averaged `r cockapoo_likes` likes, compared with `r cons_likes` for
conservative-coded videos, indicating that individuals are seemingly
less likely to seek out content related to conservative social topics.
The number of followers was also greater among cockapoo-related content
creators `` `r cockapoo_followers` ``, compared to conservative-coded
social content creators, `` `r cons_followers` ``. However, since only
one out of the four rounds contained cockapoo content, these results are
somewhat limited in generalizability, as the variance in background
attributes is likely higher within the group that has a smaller sample
size; that is, the cockapoo condition.
